2. Markdown
In your document, describe your PhD project with a ### heading, one bold and one italic word, a 3-item list and a link to your lab.

title: Session 1: Exercises
text:
3. Vectors
Stroop task, one participant, RT in ms:

rt <- c(523, 487, 601, 455, 2310, 512, 498, 577, 466, 540)
condition <- c("cong", "incong", "incong", "cong", "incong",
               "cong", "incong", "incong", "cong", "cong")


Number of trials; mean, median, min, max RT.
Find the suspicious trial (which.max()). Why do mean and median differ?
Create rt_clean without trials over 2000 ms. Recompute the mean.
Mean RT for "cong" and "incong" trials, without the slow one. Hint: drop it from both vectors.
Convert rt to seconds (rt_s).

title: Session 1: Exercises
text:
4. Missing values and comparisons
A second participant missed two trials:

rt2 <- c(523, NA, 487, 150, 601, 455, 2310, NA, 512, 498)


How many NAs? In which trials?
Mean RT, ignoring them.
Flag implausible trials: faster than 200 ms or slower than 1500 ms. How many? What proportion of the non-missing trials? Hint: the mean of a logical vector is a proportion.
Print rt2[rt2 > 200]. What went wrong? Keep only the trials that are both non-missing and plausible.

title: Session 1: Exercises
text:
5. Spot the bugs
This code has five mistakes. Copy it, fix it, run it. One mistake gives no error, only a wrong answer: which one?

scores <- c(12, 15, 9, 20, 17)
group <- c("a", "b", "a", "b", "a")
mean(scores[group = "a"]
maen(scores[group == "b"])
Mean(scores)
summary(Scores)

title: Session 1: Exercises
text:
6. Factors: a Likert item
“How often do you have trouble sleeping?”

answers <- c("often", "never", "sometimes", "always", "often", "rarely",
             "sometimes", "often", "never", "always", "sometimes", "often")


table(answers). Is the order sensible?
Make answers_f, an ordered factor with levels from "never" to "always". table() again.
Scores 1 to 5: as.numeric(answers_f). Mean score?
A new participant answers "Often". Add it, rebuild the factor. What happens, and why?

title: Session 1: Exercises
text:
8. Your first function

Write se(), the standard error of the mean, \(s/\sqrt{n}\). Use it on rt_clean.
Make it ignore NAs, and try it on rt2. Hint: sd(x, na.rm = TRUE), sum(!is.na(x)).
Write n_outliers(x, low = 200, high = 1500): the number of values below low or above high, ignoring NAs. Try n_outliers(rt2) and n_outliers(rt2, high = 600).

title: Session 1: Exercises
text:
9. A data frame: sleep
Built into R: extra hours of sleep (extra) for 10 patients (ID) under two drugs (group).

str(), head(), summary(). Rows and columns?
Mean extra per drug (tapply(), or subset twice).
Every patient took both drugs. Per patient, compute drug 2 - drug 1. How many are positive?
Write this sentence in your document, with inline code in place of the dots:

On average, drug 2 increased sleep by `{r} ...` hours more than drug 1,
and `{r} ...` out of 10 patients slept more with drug 2.

title: Session 1: Exercises
text:
10. A figure with a caption

boxplot(extra ~ group, data = sleep).
Add #| label: fig-... and #| fig-cap:. Reference it in the text with @fig-.... Render.
Add #| echo: false. What changes?

title: Session 1: Exercises
text:
11. Read data from the project
sleepstudy (Belenky et al., 2003): mean reaction time per day for 18 subjects. Days 0 and 1 were training, day 2 is the baseline. After day 2, subjects spent only 3 hours in bed per night.

read.csv(here::here("data", "sleepstudy.csv")).
How many subjects? (unique(), length())
Mean reaction time at baseline (day 2) and on day 9?
Per subject, the change from day 2 to day 9. Hint: keep the rows of day 2 and of day 9 in two data frames; check that Subject is in the same order; subtract.
How many subjects slowed down? Who slowed down the most?
hist() of the changes, with a figure caption.
One sentence with the mean change and the number of subjects who slowed down, all with inline code.

title: Session 1: Exercises

12. Does it render from scratch?

In the console, type x <- 42. In your document, add a chunk with x * 2. Render. What happens, and why?

Add a last chunk with sessionInfo().

title: Introduction
section: From a sample to general conclusions
text:
From a sample to general conclusions
We observe a tiny portion of the world, e.g. a few subjects, sessions, trials.
We want conclusions that hold in general.

Statistics quantifies how much we can generalise despite

measurement noise (scanner, electrodes, questionnaires);
variability between and within subjects;
factors we did not measure.

title: Introduction
text:
Fisher’s three ideas, in neuroscience
Study of populations

100 subjects scanned once: population across individuals.
1 subject scanned daily for a year: population across time.


Study of variation

Variability between subjects, across time, across space.



Data reduction

From millions of numbers per subject to summaries (means, components, features).

Fisher (1925), Statistical Methods for Research Workers, ch. 1

title: Introduction
section: A warning we will carry along
text:
A warning we will carry along
Classical tools (t-test, ANOVA, regression) assume independent observations.

Neuroscience data often are not:

10 trials from one subject are more similar than 10 trials from 10 subjects;
the same questionnaire filled in 6 times by one participant gives correlated scores.



Ignoring this leads to overconfidence (underestimation of uncertainty)
A standard tool to deal with correlated responses is mixed models, but they we will not cover them in this course.

title: Introduction
text:
The reproducibility crisis

Reproducibility: same data and same analysis give the same results.
Replication: new data on the same question give consistent results.



Nature survey of 1,576 researchers: more than 70% had tried and failed to replicate another scientist’s experiments, more than half their own (Baker, 2016).
70 teams analysed the same fMRI data to test the same 9 hypotheses. No two teams used the same workflow, and their results varied considerably (Botvinik-Nezer et al., 2020).



Common threats: low statistical power, trying analyses until something is significant (p-hacking), hypotheses made up after seeing the results, unpublished null results, no shared data or code (Munafò et al., 2017).

title: Introduction
text:
A starting point

State the hypothesis before looking at the data.
Share raw data and code. Every number in the paper generated automatically.
Write reports where text, code and results live together.



This is why we analyse data with code.

Basic R grammar
Run a line: Ctrl+Enter (Windows) / Cmd+Enter (Mac).

a <- 1                    # assign 1 to a (numeric value)
b <- 2
label <- "control"        # character value

trials <- 1:5                     # sequence 1 to 5
seq(0, 1, by = 0.25)              # regular sequence

title: Introduction
text:
Common mistakes
R is case-sensitive: RT and rt are different objects. Pick one style (snake_case: mean_rt).


mean(c(1, 2, 3)

Missing ): R shows + and waits. Press Esc.



maen(rt)

title: Introduction
text:
Logical values and comparisons



Operator
Meaning
Example




==, !=
equal, not equal
3 == 3 is TRUE


<, >, <=, >=
comparisons
5 > 2 is TRUE


%in%
element in a set
"a" %in% c("a","b") is TRUE


&, |, !
and, or, not
TRUE & FALSE is FALSE





rt <- c(512, 430, 1601, 488, 150)
too_fast_or_slow <- rt < 200 | rt > 1500   # flag implausible trials
rt[!too_fast_or_slow]                       # keep valid trials

[1] 512 430 488

title: Introduction
text:
Factors
Categorical variables with fixed levels:

group <- factor(c("patient", "control", "control", "patient", "control"))
levels(group)

[1] "control" "patient"

group
control patient 
      3       2 



Ordered categories (a Likert item):

answer <- c("never", "always", "often", "never")
factor(answer, levels = c("never", "often", "always"), ordered = TRUE)

[1] never  always often  never 
Levels: never < often < always

title: Introduction
text:
Data frames
One row per observation, one column per variable. Columns can have different types.

subjects <- data.frame(
  id    = c("S01", "S02", "S03", "S04"),
  group = factor(c("patient", "control", "patient", "control")),
  age   = c(64, 58, 71, 60),
  mmse  = c(22, 29, 19, 28)
)
subjects

1 S01 patient  64   22
2 S02 control  58   29
3 S03 patient  71   19
4 S04 control  60   28

title: Introduction
Introduction
text:
Anatomy of a .qmd file
---
title: "Sleep deprivation: first look"
author: "Your Name"
format: html
---

## Data

```{r}
#| echo: false
sleepstudy <- read.csv(here::here("data", "sleepstudy.csv"))
```

The dataset contains `{r} nrow(sleepstudy)` measurements.

YAML header between ---: title, author, format (html, docx, typst).
Markdown text: ## Section, **bold**, *italic*, - lists, $\bar x$.
Code chunks: run at render; options start with #|.
Inline code: numbers inside sentences, never typed by hand.

title: Introduction
text:
Rendering and chunk options
Render: Ctrl/Cmd + Shift + K. The file runs from scratch: it must load its own packages and data.








Option
Effect




#| echo: false
hide code, show results


#| eval: false
show code, don’t run it


#| include: false
run, show nothing


#| label: fig-rt and #| fig-cap: "..."
numbered figure, cite with @fig-rt
